1.0-1

Matter stores quantum states and photons carry them

  • The stationary qubits, atoms, ions and spins, store the quantum state
  • Photons, the flying qubits, carry the state from node to node
  • Small processors linked by photons make one modular processor
  • Repeaters carry entanglement farther than a photon sent directly can go
  • The interface moves the state between matter and a photon, both ways
Kimble, Nature 453, 1023 (2008), arXiv:0806.4195; Wehner, Elkouss and Hanson, Science 362, eaam9288 (2018)
1.0-2

A network of quantum nodes does what no single node can

  • Distant users share a secret key whose security rests on physics
  • A user runs a program on a remote quantum computer and keeps it private
  • Entangled clocks in separate laboratories act as one more stable clock
  • Small processors joined by photons compute as one large processor
  • From the third stage up, the nodes share entanglement
Wehner, Elkouss and Hanson, Science 362, eaam9288 (2018), Fig. 4 and Table 1; Kómár et al., Nat. Phys. 10, 582 (2014), arXiv:1310.6045; Monroe et al., Phys. Rev. A 89, 022317 (2014), arXiv:1208.0391
1.0-3

A neutral-atom quantum computer needs links between arrays

  • The largest tweezer array holds 6100 atoms in 12 000 traps
  • One objective and its laser power limit a module to about 104 atoms
  • Larger machines join modules by entangled atom pairs made through photons
  • Modules need about 106 pairs per second (projected); links make hundreds
  • The lab's design study joins seven modules of about 104 traps by 21 fibre links
Manetsch et al., Nature 647, 60 (2025), arXiv:2403.12021; Sunami et al., PRX Quantum 6, 010101 (2025), arXiv:2407.11111; Sinclair et al., Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025), arXiv:2408.08955; Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088

1.0-5

Links between matter nodes reach tens of kilometres

  • Awschalom et al. name three scales: on a chip, between modules, and 0.1 to 1000 km
  • At metres, ions and NVs make links faster than the links decohere
  • With frequency conversion of the photon, ions and atoms reach 33 to 100 km of fibre
Awschalom et al., PRX Quantum 2, 017002 (2021), arXiv:1912.06642; the links: sections 2.6 to 2.8, and Lu et al., Science 391, 592 (2026), arXiv:2602.09596
1.0-6

The links quantum networks need are still to be built

  • No two arrays of neutral atoms have been linked through cavities
  • No two superconducting qubits have been entangled through light
  • Over kilometres, no link yet makes pairs faster than they decay
  • Links make hundreds of pairs per second; modules need about 106, projected
  • A repeater has beaten ideal direct transmission only over an emulated loss
The first two hold as far as published work shows in November 2026, the others among the experiments of these lectures. Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088; Sunami et al., PRX Quantum 6, 010101 (2025), arXiv:2407.11111; Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), arXiv:1909.01323
1.0-7

Four kinds of interface put light and atom in one mode

  • (a) A cavity of two mirrors
  • (b) An optical nanofibre
  • (c) A waveguide on a chip
  • (d) A resonator beside a guide
  • In a guide the atom emits into the mode at Γ1D and elsewhere at Γ′ (1.3)
  • In a cavity the coupling g competes with the losses κ and γ (1.4)
1.0-8

Every platform is judged on the same figures of merit

ηlink=γent/γdec
  • A share β of the atom's emission enters the mode; in a cavity C1 sets it
  • A fraction η of the photons is collected and detected
  • Links are made at γent, the success probability per attempt times f
  • A fidelity is quoted with its success probability
  • A stored link decays at the rate γdec
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023), arXiv:2304.02088
1.0-9

What the two lectures teach

  • How much of a light beam one atom can take, and what sets the limit
  • How many atoms, a waveguide and a cavity each raise the coupling
  • How the coupling makes a memory, a source of single photons and a gate
  • How two distant nodes are entangled through photons, and at what rate
  • How ions, atoms, colour centres and circuits compare on one set of figures of merit

1.0-13
1.1

One atom and light

The driven two-level atom · Rabi oscillations · Γ and γ · saturation · the cross section · one atom in a focused beam

1.1

A laser couples the ground and excited levels of the atom

Hint=−ℏΩ2(e−iωLt|e⟩⟨g|+h.c.)
Ω=𝐝eg·𝐄0/ℏ,Δ=ωL−ω0
  • Ω is the full Rabi frequency
  • 𝐄0 is the field amplitude and ωL the laser frequency
  • Δ is the detuning, drawn here below resonance
  • |e⟩ decays by spontaneous emission at the rate Γ
Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-1

The atom flops between the levels, less fully off resonance

Pe(t)=Ω2Ω′2sin2(Ω′t2)
Ω′=Ω2+Δ2
  • On resonance a pulse of area Ωt=π fills |e⟩
  • Off resonance it flops faster, at Ω′, and only up to Ω2/Ω′2
  • The curves leave out decay and hold for t≪1/Γ
Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-2

Spontaneous emission sets the linewidth Γ

Γ=1τ=Aeg=ω03|deg|23πε0ℏc3
γ=Γ/2
  • The excited state decays at the rate Γ; the natural linewidth is Γ/2π
  • The dipole, and with it the optical coherence, decays at γ=Γ/2
  • Rubidium D₂ line: Γ/2π=6.07 MHz and τ=26.2 ns
Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7; Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-3

Strong driving saturates the scattering rate at Γ/2

s=IIsat=2Ω2Γ2
R=Γ2s1+s+4Δ2/Γ2
  • Rubidium D₂, σ± cycling transition: Isat=1.67 mW/cm²
  • From here on s≪1, as for a single photon
  • A classical drive is coherent when Ω≫γ
  • One photon needs nearly all the atom's light in its mode, the aim of the sections ahead
Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7; Foot, Atomic Physics (Oxford University Press, 2005), ch. 7
1.1-4

One atom blocks an area 3λ²/2π of resonant light

σ0=ℏω0Γ2Isat=3λ22π
σ(Δ)=σ01+4Δ2/Γ2
  • σ0 is the rate R at s≪1 over the photon flux I/ℏω0
  • Γ and Isat both grow as |deg|2, so the dipole cancels
  • σ0 holds for a closed transition driven with matched polarisation
  • Rubidium D₂, σ± cycling transition: σ0=2.91×10−9 cm², or 0.29 µm²
Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7, Eqs. 50, 52 and 61
1.1-5

An atom removes light from a beam by interference

  • A share β of the atom's light enters the beam's mode, opposite in phase: amplitude −β
  • Behind the atom the probe's 1 becomes 1−β, so 1−T≈2β for β≪1
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eqs. 52 and 53; Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, Eq. 58
1.1-6

A tighter focus gives the atom a larger share of the beam

1−T=2β,β≈σ02A
A=πW022,zR=πW02λ
  • W0 is the waist radius of the Gaussian beam
  • β is the share of the atom's light that goes into the beam's mode
  • The waist keeps its size only over the Rayleigh range zR
  • In an ordinary beam β is about 10−4
  • A guided mode, drawn below, keeps its small area over any length
β about 10⁻⁴: Windpassinger et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 100, 103601 (2008), arXiv:0801.4126, as quoted by Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824, Sec. II.A
1.1-7

One atom in a focused beam removes a tenth of the light

  • One 87Rb atom is held at the focus of two aspheric lenses of NA 0.55
  • The probe beam is focused to a waist of about 0.86 µm
  • On resonance the atom removes 9.8 ± 0.2 % of the probe
  • Since 1−T=2β, this is β≈5 %
Tey et al., Nat. Phys. 4, 924 (2008), arXiv:0802.3005
1.1-8

The measured extinction is well below the paraxial estimate

  • At W0=0.86 µm the paraxial formula gives 2β=σ0/A=0.25
  • The paper's full-field model predicts 20 %
  • The measured extinction is 9.8 ± 0.2 %, so β≈5 %
  • The authors ascribe the shortfall from 20 % to the lens and the atom's motion
Tey et al., Nat. Phys. 4, 924 (2008), arXiv:0802.3005; σ₀: Steck, Rubidium 87 D Line Data, rev. 2.3.4 (8 Aug 2025), Tables 3 and 7
1.1-9
1.2

Many atoms in free space: optical depth and the memory

Beer's law and OD · the Λ system and EIT · slow light and storage · efficiency against OD · why a waveguide

1.2

A cloud of atoms attenuates light exponentially

I(z)=I0e−αz,α=nσ
OD=αL=nσ0L=−lnT
  • n is the atom density and σ the cross section
  • On resonance σ0=3λ2/2π (section 1.1)
  • T is the transmitted fraction of a weak resonant probe
  • Only the column density nL enters
  • Some papers use d=OD/2 instead (Gorshkov 2007)
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083, for d = OD/2
1.2-1

Two fields on a Λ system leave one state dark

|D⟩=Ωc|g⟩−Ωp|f⟩Ωc2+Ωp2
  • The probe Ωp drives |g⟩ to |e⟩, the control Ωc drives |f⟩ to |e⟩
  • In |D⟩ the two paths to |e⟩ cancel, so it does not scatter
  • |D⟩ exists only at two-photon resonance
  • The coherence of |g⟩ and |f⟩ decays at the rate γgf
  • This is the dark state of one atom, not of the ensemble
Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003)
1.2-2

A strong control opens a transparent window in the line

Ωc2≫ΓγgfWEIT≈Ωc2ΓOD
  • Without the control the probe is absorbed over the full width Γ
  • With it a window opens at two-photon resonance, δ=0
  • A control with Ωc>Γ splits the line into an Autler-Townes doublet
  • The window narrows as OD grows
  • Across it n rises steeply, so vg=c/(n+ωdn/dω)≪c
Lvovsky, Sanders and Tittel, Nat. Photonics 3, 706 (2009), arXiv:1002.4659, Eq. 1; Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003), Eq. 2 and Fig. 1
1.2-3

Slowed light is a photon shared with a spin wave

  • The pulse moves at vg=LΩc2/(Γ·OD); the mixing angle is tanθ=2gN/Ωc
  • g couples one atom to one probe photon; N atoms sharing one excitation couple with gN
Fleischhauer and Lukin, Phys. Rev. Lett. 84, 5094 (2000), arXiv:quant-ph/0001094; Lukin, Rev. Mod. Phys. 75, 457 (2003), Eq. 15
1.2-4

A pulse is stored whole only if it fits in the medium

τd=Lvg=Γ·ODΩc2
τdWEIT≈OD
  • Inside, a pulse of length cτ shrinks to vgτ
  • It fits only if vgτ<L, that is τ<τd
  • Its spectrum must fit the window, 1/τ<WEIT
  • Both hold only if 1<τd/τ<OD
  • A large optical depth leaves room for both
Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, after Eq. 1 and supplement Eq. S21; Lvovsky, Sanders and Tittel, Nat. Photonics 3, 706 (2009), arXiv:1002.4659, Eq. 1
1.2-5

Read-out is collective emission into the forward mode

Γfwd~NβΓ=OD2Γ
1−ηmem~ΓΓfwd~2OD
  • On read-out each atom radiates with the phase of the probe at its place
  • Forward, in the probe mode, the waves of all N atoms add up
  • Into every other direction each atom emits alone, at Γ
  • β=σ0/2A is one atom's share of the mode (section 1.1)
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083, Sec. III and Fig. 2
1.2-6

The memory error falls as one over the optical depth

1−ηmem≈5.8/OD
1−ηmem≈12/OD  or  38/OD
  • 5.8/OD is the error of storage alone or of retrieval alone
  • 12/OD is the error of storage followed by backward retrieval
  • 38/OD is the error of storage followed by forward retrieval
  • All are asymptotic fits of the optimum, the same for EIT, Raman and echo memories
  • ηmem, the energy retrieved over the energy sent in, is an efficiency, not a fidelity
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083, Fig. 4; Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, Fig. 4(d); Vernaz-Gris et al., Nat. Commun. 9, 363 (2018), arXiv:1707.09372; Chanelière, Hétet and Sangouard, arXiv 1801.10023 (2018)
1.2-7

Hsiao 2018 stored and retrieved 92 % of the light at OD 816

  • Storage and retrieval efficiency 92.0(1.5) % at OD 816
  • Classical probe pulses of 200 ns with about 30 000 photons each, not single photons
  • The paper notes that it could be extended to the quantum regime
  • The storage time at 50 % efficiency is 1200 pulse durations, the time-bandwidth product
  • At OD 550 the efficiency decays with storage time, τ = 325 µs
Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, Figs. 3 and 4(d)
1.2-8

The optical depth fixes the number of atoms in the beam

N=nAL=OD·Aσ0
  • A=πW02/2 is the beam area of section 1.1; the length L drops out
  • A waist of 100 µm at 780 nm gives A/σ0≈5×104
  • OD 800 then needs about 4×107 atoms in the beam
  • OD 58, a one-way error of 10 %, needs about 3×106
  • Hsiao's whole trap held about 5×109 atoms, a node of Yu 2020 about 108
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083; Hsiao et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 120, 183602 (2018), arXiv:1605.08519, supplement; Yu et al., Nature 578, 240 (2020), arXiv:1903.11284
1.2-9

Free space cannot give a small area and a long length

ODN=σ0Amode
zR=πW02/λ
  • The same OD from fewer atoms needs a smaller mode area
  • A focused beam keeps its small area only within ±zR of the focus
  • So a tight focus is short, and few atoms fit in it
  • A guided mode keeps a small area over any length L
  • Along a waveguide OD≈2Nβ (section 1.3)
Solano et al., Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 66, 439 (2017), arXiv:1703.10533, Eqs. 5 and 6
1.2-10
1.3

Waveguide QED

Decay channels and β · one atom in a waveguide · β and C₁ · β across platforms · the memory on a waveguide · super- and subradiance · ordered arrays and chiral emission

1.3

A waveguide takes a fraction β of the emitter's decay

Γtot=Γ1D+Γ′
β=Γ1DΓ1D+Γ′
  • Γ1D is the decay rate into the guided mode, both directions together
  • Γ′ is the rate into every other channel
  • β is the probability that an emitted photon is guided
  • Γ′ is not Γ: calculated, 1.3Γ on a nanofibre and 0.8 to 1.1Γ on photonic crystals
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eq. 51; Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382; Bouscal et al., New J. Phys. 26, 023026 (2024), arXiv:2301.04675; Hood et al., Proc. Natl Acad. Sci. USA 113, 10507 (2016), arXiv:1603.02771
1.3-1

One atom passes 1 − β of the field and reflects −β

s=−Γ1D/2Γtot/2=−β
t=1+s=1−β,r=s=−β
  • Driven weakly on resonance, the atom scatters s both ways, in antiphase with the incident wave
  • Forward, the scattered wave adds to the incident one; backward, it is all there is
  • The guide keeps T=(1−β)2 and R=β2; the rest, 2β(1−β), is lost
  • At β=0.3, 49 % passes, 9 % returns and 42 % is lost
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eqs. 52 and 53 (T and R at zero dephasing)
1.3-2

A weakly coupled atom removes 2β of the guided power

T=(1−β)2≈1−2β
TN=TN,OD=−lnTN≈2Nβ
  • Each atom removes 2β of the power when β≪1
  • N atoms in a row, reflections between them neglected, transmit TN=TN
  • The reflection, β2, is second order and drops out
  • The loss 2β(1−β) reaches one half at β=1/2
  • At β=1 the atom reflects everything, R=1
  • The dotted line marks the example β=0.3
Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eqs. 52 and 53 at zero dephasing
1.3-3

β and C₁ are two names for one ratio of rates

C1=12β1−β=Γ1D2Γ′
β=2C11+2C1
  • Half the emission is guided when C1=1/2
  • The ratio of the rates Γ1D/Γ′=β/(1−β) is 2C1
  • A cooperativity defined as β/(1−β) or g2/(κγ) is therefore 2C1
  • In a cavity, 2C1/(1+2C1) is the share of the emission into the cavity mode
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 4 (C₁ = g²/(2κγ), κ and γ half widths)
1.3-4

Γ1D grows with the guided field at the atom

Γ1D∝|𝐝·𝐄(𝐫)|2
  • Γ1D is largest where the guided field is strongest and lies along the dipole
  • The atom couples through the evanescent tail outside the glass, strongest at an optimal radius
  • A slow guided mode, of high group index, raises Γ1D
  • "Purcell factor" means Γ1D/Γ or Γtot/Γ, by paper
Calculated from the exact HE₁₁ mode (Le Kien et al., Phys. Rev. A 72, 063815 (2005)); Solano et al., Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 66, 439 (2017), arXiv:1703.10533; Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015), arXiv:1312.1079, Eq. 49
1.3-5

On a nanofibre β falls steeply with distance from the glass

  • The blue curve is β for a fibre 300 nm in diameter, calculated
  • β falls from about 20 % at the surface to under 1 % at 0.8 µm
  • The red curve is a tweezer's trapping potential; its minima are the trapping sites
  • β is 10 % at the first site, about 190 nm out, and 1.4 % at the second
  • The paper writes η for β
Figure: Nayak, Wang and Keloth, Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 213602 (2019), arXiv:1908.03319, Fig. 1(d), calculated after Le Kien et al., Phys. Rev. A 72, 032509 (2005)

Pache 2025165 ± 136.9 ± 0.82.1 % (β=1.1±0.2 % forward)
  • Each β is OD/2N, Corzo's apart; in brackets, each paper's own measure of the coupling
  • Pache 2025 counts only the forward direction in its β, so that OD=4βN
  • Corzo 2019 also stored one heralded excitation and retrieved it as a guided photon with an efficiency of 25 ± 3 %
Vetsch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 203603 (2010), arXiv:0912.1179; Corzo et al., Nature 566, 359 (2019), arXiv:1909.08641; Han et al., arXiv 2509.22958 (2025), preprint; Pache et al., Phys. Rev. A 112, L011701 (2025), arXiv:2407.02278
1.3-8

On a waveguide the memory error falls as 1/(Nβ)

OD≈2Nβ,D=2NΓ1DΓ′=4NC1
1−ηmem≈5.8OD≈2.9Nβ
  • The exact form D equals 2Nβ when β≪1
  • The waveguide replaces N by Nβ and keeps the 1/N scaling
  • At the lab's design value β=0.05, an error of 1 % one way needs about 6000 atoms
  • Vetsch 2010 trapped two rows of atoms along a fibre 500 nm thick
Figure: Vetsch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 203603 (2010), arXiv:0912.1179, Fig. 2; Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083; Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382
1.3-9

Two atoms in phase emit into the guide twice as fast

Γ±=Γ′+Γ1D(1±1)ΓN=Γ′+NΓ1D
Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824, Eqs. 15 to 17; rates of one atom at a nanofibre, calculated: Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382
1.3-10

A spin wave outside the light cone does not radiate

  • A spin wave in an ordered array of spacing d has a wavenumber k up to π/d
  • For |k|>k0=ω0/c the wavelets cancel, and it does not radiate
  • The guided mode lies outside the cone too, at k1D
  • One spin wave can be subradiant into free space and superradiant into the guide
Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382; the band diagram is schematic, the maps calculated for scalar waves
1.3-11

Selective radiance sends one collective mode into the guide

  • The guided rate Γ1D (blue) peaks at ±k1D
  • Outside the light cone, shaded grey, the rate Γ′ (green) into free space vanishes
  • The best branching ratio Γ1D/Γ′ grows as 0.0053N2, calculated
  • Such a mode is subradiant into free space and superradiant into the guide
Figure: Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382, Fig. 15, CC BY
1.3-12

Collective storage in an array can beat 1/N, in theory

  • Independent atoms lose 5.8/D≈10/N
  • A spin wave whose population grows as j2 along the chain loses about 26/N2
  • A Gaussian spin wave under a uniform control field loses 4.1/N
  • Under a control rising towards the exit it loses 0.15e−N/23
  • Calculated for Γ1D≈0.4Γ, Γ′≈1.3Γ and d=λ1D/4
Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), arXiv:1703.03382, Eqs. 26 and 29, Figs. 14(c), 16(d) and 18(d); Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083
1.3-13

Guided light can be chiral and couple atoms at any range

  • Near the glass the guided field rotates, one way for each direction: chiral coupling
  • In the half-W1 design of (a), 92 % goes forward, calculated
  • Solano 2017's experiment measured superradiant decay at 1.10±0.02Γ, OD 0.66
  • About 1000 atoms on a nanofibre emit a superradiant burst
Left: calculated from the exact HE₁₁ mode for the nanofibre of Lodahl et al., Nature 541, 473 (2017), arXiv:1608.00446, Fig. 2. Figure (a): Bouscal et al., New J. Phys. 26, 023026 (2024), arXiv:2301.04675, Fig. 4(a); Solano et al., Nat. Commun. 8, 1857 (2017), arXiv:1704.07486; Liedl et al., Phys. Rev. X 14, 011020 (2024), arXiv:2211.08940
1.3-14
1.4

Cavity QED and the cavity gate

Why a cavity helps · the Fabry-Pérot · g, κ, γ and C₁ · the regimes · inhibited emission · vacuum STIRAP · a photon detected without loss · the reflection gate · memory in a cavity

1.4

A cavity brings the photon back to the atom 2F/π times

OD1=σ0πw02/2=3λ2π2w02
2FπOD1=6Fλ2π3w02=2C1
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 1; Webb et al., Nano Convergence 13, 35 (2026), p. 4 and Eq. 7
1.4-1

A Fabry-Pérot transmits a comb of narrow lines

FSR=c2L,FWHM=FSRF
F=π(R1R2)1/41−R1R2,κ=πc2LF
  • R1 and R2 are the power reflectivities of the mirrors
  • For two mirrors of R near 1, F≈π/(1−R)
  • κ is the half width in angular frequency, κ=πFWHM
  • The field decays at the rate κ, the stored energy at 2κ
1.4-2

The mirror curvature sets the waist of the mode

0≤(1−Lρ1)(1−Lρ2)≤1
w02=λ2πL(2ρ−L)(ρ1=ρ2=ρ)
  • ρ1 and ρ2 are the mirrors' radii of curvature, positive for a concave mirror
  • The mode is stable only in this range
  • A short cavity with strongly curved mirrors gives a small waist
  • The standing-wave TEM00 mode has the volume V=πw02L/4
Saleh and Teich, Fundamentals of Photonics (Wiley, 1991), Eqs. 9.2-14 and 9.2-16; Hunger et al., New J. Phys. 12, 065038 (2010), arXiv:1005.0067, Eqs. 6 and 9
1.4-3

Finesse and waist alone set the cooperativity

g=dω/(2ℏε0V)u(𝐫)
C1=g22κγ=3Fλ2π3w02
  • g=dE1/ℏ at an antinode: the Rabi frequency of one photon of field E1
  • κ and γ=Γ/2 are both half widths
  • The length cancels: g2 and κ both fall as 1/L
  • g2/(κγ) and β/(1−β) are both 2C1
  • Papers that use full widths write 2C1 as 4g2/(κΓ)
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eqs. 2 and 4; Hunger et al., New J. Phys. 12, 065038 (2010), arXiv:1005.0067, Eq. 22; Norcia, PhD thesis (2017), p. 98
1.4-4

Fibre-tip mirrors shrink the mode to a few λ³

Hunger et al. 2010Value
Finesse F37 000 ± 5000 measured (85 ± 12 ppm loss per mirror); 130 000 or more projected
Smallest mode, calculatedw0=1.3 µm and V≈5.5λ3 for ρ=50 µm, L≈2 µm
Fibre-to-cavity mode matching ε10.72 or more measured, about 0.85 realistic, 0.979 in theory
Cooperativity C1 for Rb, calculated4560 (the paper's C0) at w0=1.3 µm and the projected F
Hunger et al., New J. Phys. 12, 065038 (2010), arXiv:1005.0067
1.4-5

With C₁ > 1, a single atom changes the cavity

Nc=1C1=2κγg2,nc=γ22g2
CN=NC1
  • Nc atoms change the cavity's response noticeably
  • nc photons in the mode saturate the atom
  • For C1>1, Nc<1: a single atom is enough
  • N atoms at antinodes couple as one dipole, with gN
  • Atoms spread along the axis give CN=NC1/2
Further reading: Tanji-Suzuki et al., Adv. At. Mol. Opt. Phys. 60, 201 (2011), arXiv:1104.3594, sections 1.2 and 1.4
1.4-6

Atom and mode form a ladder of doublets split by 2g√n

H/ℏ=ωaσ+σ−+ωca†a+g(aσ++a†σ−)
En,±/ℏ=nω±gn(ωa=ωc=ω)
  • Each pair |g,n⟩, |e,n−1⟩ mixes into a doublet
  • The splitting 2gn grows with the photon number n
  • An excited atom in the empty cavity oscillates, Pe(t)=cos2(gt)
  • The lowest doublet shows as two lines 2g apart when g≫κ,γ
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 2; Haroche and Raimond, Exploring the Quantum (Oxford, 2006)
1.4-7

Strong coupling splits the line; the Purcell regime broadens it

γc=g2κ=2C1γ
Pout=κoutκ2C11+2C1
  • (a) For g≫κ,γ the line splits into two peaks at ±g, each about κ+γ wide
  • (b) For κ≫g≫γ and C1≳1 the atom's line broadens from γ to γ(1+2C1)
  • Drawn for (g,κ,γ)/2π=(7,2.5,3) MHz in (a), for κ=10g and C1=2 in (b)
  • The cavity is overcoupled when the output mirror dominates, κout≫κloss=κ−κout
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Fig. 6 and Eqs. 13 and 16
1.4-8

A cavity can also inhibit spontaneous emission

γc=g2κκ2+Δac2
γ=Γ2(1−ζ4π)
  • Δac is the detuning; on resonance γc=2C1γ
  • Detuned by many κ, emission into the mode is suppressed
  • Mirrors covering a solid angle ζ lower γ
  • Plates closer than λ/2 made an atom live at least 20 times longer (Hulet 1985)
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 12; Purcell, Phys. Rev. 69, 681 (1946); Kleppner, Phys. Rev. Lett. 47, 233 (1981); Hulet, Hilfer and Kleppner, Phys. Rev. Lett. 55, 2137 (1985)
1.4-9

A cavity and a waveguide share β = 2C₁/(1 + 2C₁)

β=γcγc+γ=2C11+2C1
C1=β2(1−β)
  • In a cavity the atom decays at γc into the mode and at γ elsewhere
  • In a waveguide it decays at Γ1D into the guide and at Γ′ elsewhere
  • For large C1 the lost share is 1−β≈1/(2C1)
  • The waveguides are plotted at their β, the cavities at their C1
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889; Sheremet et al., Rev. Mod. Phys. 95, 015002 (2023), arXiv:2103.06824; Pache et al., Phys. Rev. A 112, L011701 (2025), arXiv:2407.02278
1.4-10

A dark state of atom and cavity carries a photon in and out

tanθ=Ω2g
  • The control laser Ω couples |g⟩ to |e⟩, the cavity's g couples |e⟩ to |f⟩
  • Their dark state has no part in |e⟩: it is |g,0⟩ for Ω≪2g and |f,1⟩ for Ω≫2g
  • STIRAP, stimulated Raman adiabatic passage: a slow Ω keeps the state dark
  • The |f,1⟩ part leaks out at 2κ as a photon shaped by Ω(t); reversed, it absorbs one
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, section I.E, Eq. 19; emission and absorption, sections III.A and IV.A.1; Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), arXiv:1202.5955
1.4-11

Two single-atom nodes passed a qubit by vacuum STIRAP

  • A qubit passed from atom to atom with fidelity 84(1) % at 0.2 % success
  • A lower bound, post-selected: a success shows only when the read-out photon is detected
Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), arXiv:1202.5955
1.4-12

A Rydberg atom detects a photon without absorbing it

  • A cavity at 51.1 GHz, photon lifetime 1 ms, couples g to e but not i
  • With one photon, g makes one full Rabi cycle, 2gt=2π: |⁠g⁠,⁠1⁠⟩⁠ ⁠→⁠ ⁠−⁠|⁠g⁠,⁠1⁠⟩
  • The Ramsey zones R1 and R2, two π/2 pulses, turn that sign into the level g or i
  • The photon stays in the cavity, and a second atom detects it again
  • One quantum sets a π phase, as in the coming gate; here it is read on the atom
Figure: Nogues et al., Nature 400, 239 (1999), Fig. 1 (left); Gleyzes et al., Nature 446, 297 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612031; Guerlin et al., Nature 448, 889 (2007), arXiv:0707.3880
1.4-13

On resonance an atom turns the reflection from −1 to +1

r(Δ)=1−2κin(γ+iΔ)(κ+iΔ)(γ+iΔ)+g2
r(0)=2C1−12C1+1(κloss=0)
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 16, with no transmission through the back mirror
1.4-14

The π phase shift needs a one-sided cavity with 2C₁ > 1

  • The light leaves only through the input mirror: κin≫κloss
  • The pulse spectrum is narrower than κ, and the beam is matched to the cavity mode
  • Plotted for (g,κ,γ)/2π=(6.7,2.5,3) MHz, where C1≈3
  • At this C1 the atom still scatters 0.49 of the pulse
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eq. 16; g, κ, γ of Reiserer et al., Nature 508, 237 (2014), arXiv:1404.2453
1.4-15

One reflection changes the sign of one atom-photon state

  • The atom's |⁠↑⁠⟩ couples to the cavity; |⁠↓⁠⟩, a hyperfine splitting lower, does not
  • A controlled phase flip: only |⁠h⁠↓⁠⟩, h in the cavity and the atom uncoupled, changes sign
Duan and Kimble, Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 127902 (2004), arXiv:quant-ph/0309187, Fig. 1
1.4-16

Reflections off one atom make a controlled phase flip

  • The controlled phase flip of two photons changes the sign of |hh⟩ alone
  • A photon lost by spontaneous emission, Ps≈1/(1+C1), gives no click: heralded
Duan and Kimble, Phys. Rev. Lett. 92, 127902 (2004), arXiv:quant-ph/0309187, Eq. 1 and Fig. 2
1.4-17

One reflection gave the first atom-photon quantum gate

  • One 87Rb atom, (g,κ,γ)/2π=(6.7,2.5,3) MHz: C1≈3; all results post-selected
  • Truth table (left): atom ↑ (coupled) or ↓, photon ↑ˣ or ↓ˣ; right in 99 % (↓), 86 % (↑)
  • The photon is not reflected in 30(2) % (uncoupled) and 34(2) % (coupled)
  • Atom and photon in ↓ˣ become the Bell state (⁠|⁠↑⁠↑⁠ˣ⁠⟩⁠ ⁠+⁠ ⁠|⁠↓⁠↓⁠ˣ⁠⟩⁠)⁠/⁠√⁠2: 80.7(5) % at n¯=0.07
  • A second photon gives the GHZ state (⁠|⁠↑⁠↑⁠ˣ⁠↑⁠ˣ⁠⟩⁠ ⁠−⁠ ⁠|⁠↓⁠↓⁠ˣ⁠↓⁠ˣ⁠⟩⁠)⁠/⁠√⁠2: 61(2) %
Figure: Reiserer et al., Nature 508, 237 (2014), arXiv:1404.2453, Fig. 1b (left) and Fig. 2 (right)
1.4-18

A nanophotonic cavity showed the same π phase switch

  • One atom beside a nanophotonic cavity: C1=3.9 [the paper's η=7.7±0.3 is 2C1]
  • The atom shifts the phase of a weak reflected probe by (1.1±0.1)π (left)
  • A gate pulse of n¯≈0.6 photons shifts the atom's phase by (0.98±0.07)π (right)
  • Both post-selected: on an atom in the cavity, and on a reflected gate photon
Figure: Tiecke et al., Nature 508, 241 (2014), arXiv:1404.5615, Fig. 2a (left) and Fig. 4b (right)
1.4-19

Light outside the cavity mode reflects as off a plain mirror

Rexp=(1−ξ)+ξ|r|2
  • A fraction ξ of the input power is in the cavity mode
  • That part comes back as |r|2; the cavity's reflection coefficient r depends on the atom
  • The rest, 1−ξ, never meets the atom and carries no atom-dependent phase
  • Mode overlap in Reiserer 2014: 92(3) %
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, pp. 9 to 10; mode overlap: Reiserer et al., Nature 508, 237 (2014), arXiv:1404.2453
1.4-20

In a cavity the memory efficiency is set by CN, not by OD

ηmem=(2CN1+2CN)2
  • Each step has 2CN/(1+2CN): the β of a cavity, with the ensemble's CN for C1
  • Retrieval is emission into the mode against loss to the side; storage is its reverse
  • CN=NC1 for atoms at antinodes, in the bad-cavity limit κ≫gN
  • Free space gives 1−5.8/OD per step, 1−12/OD for both read backwards
  • One atom at C1=25 gives 98 % per step and about 96 % for both
Cavity: Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033804 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612082; free space: Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007), arXiv:quant-ph/0612083
1.4-21

Cavity experiments reach C₁ from 0.22 to 145

  • Each value is C1 with half widths; the paper's own value, where it differs, in brackets
  • The open marker, from a preprint, is an internal cooperativity, with κloss in place of κ
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, and the experiments named in the figure
1.4-22

An interface needs large C₁, an overcoupled cavity and mode matching

Pout=κoutκ·2C11+2C1
  • Pout is the share of the atom's emission that leaves by the output mirror
  • A large C1, g2 large against κγ, sends the emission into the cavity mode
  • That share is β=2C1/(1+2C1), the number a waveguide is judged by
  • In an overcoupled cavity, κout≫κloss, the escape factor κout/κ is near 1
  • Mode matching, ξ→1, keeps the incoming light from bypassing the atom
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), arXiv:1412.2889, Eqs. 4, 13 and 20; mode matching pp. 9 to 10
1.4-23

Summary of lecture 1

  • One atom takes β≈σ0/2A of a focused beam
  • Tey 2008: 9.8 ± 0.2 % extinction by one atom
  • Many atoms: OD=nσ0L, memory error 5.8/OD
  • A waveguide: β=Γ1D/(Γ1D+Γ′), OD≈2Nβ
  • A cavity: C1=g2/(2κγ), β=2C1/(1+2C1)
  • If 2C1>1, one atom flips the sign of the reflection r

Lecture 2 judges each platform on the same figures of merit

  • Lecture 2 opens on heralded links and the repeater (2.5)
  • Sections 2.6 to 2.9 take one platform each
  • Section 2.10 gives the benchmarks and one example from the lab
  • The problem set is handed out today; Problems 1 and 2 can be answered now
  • Problem 2 uses the fibre Fabry-Pérot cavity of 1.4; Problem 3 needs lecture 2
